title: Lab 3: Linear Regression Model Comparisons
text:
Load and clean the dataset


Code
data <- attitude

data.clean <- attitude |>
  select(rating, complaints, learning, raises) |>
  drop_na()

n <- nrow(data.clean)


The data set attitude is a build-in R data set that includes overall workplace ratings from 30 departments. Handling of employee complaints, opportunity to learn, and pay raises will be used as predictor variables.
The final analysis included all 30 departments.
It is expected that the handling of workplace complaints be positively associated with overall workplace ratings because it shows that any problems seen in the workplace are being addressed. Opportunities for learning are expected to be positively associated with overall workplace rating beyond handling of complaints as more opportunities can give employees a sense of growth and accomplishment and make them more satisfied with their job. Pay increase is expected to be positively associated with workplace rating above and beyond the other two variables because even if complaints are dealt with and learning is fostered, it is unlikely that employees would rate a workplace positively if they are not being fairly compensated for their improvement and inflation.

title: Lab 3: Linear Regression Model Comparisons
text:
Create and Evaluate Competing Models
Nested models will be created starting at the intercept and increasing in complexity as more variables are added to the previous model.








Model
Formula
Research rationale




M0: Null
rating ~ 1
Baseline model


M1: Complaints
rating ~ complaints
Evaluate complaint handling


M2: Complaints + Learning
rating ~ complaints + learning
Evaluate the additional contribution of learning


M3: Expanded
rating ~ complaints + learning + raises
Evaluate the additional contribution of pay raises




Fit the Nested Models


Code
# Intercept-only model
model_1 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = data.clean)

# complaints model
model_2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = data.clean)

# complaints + learning model
model_3 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = data.clean)

# Expanded model
model_4 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = data.clean)

In Model 1, the intercept represents the sample mean occupational rating. In Model 2, the complaints coefficient represents the expected increase in rating associated with one additional rating of average complaint handling. In Model 3, the complaints coefficient represents this increase after adjusting for the rating of opportunity for learning. While the increase lowers, complaints remains a significant predictor of overall rating. Learning has a non-significant association with rating when complaints are held constant, but the addition of learning slightly increases the variance explained by the model. In Model 4, complaints and learning coefficients are additionally adjusted for pay raises. Learning and pay rises both have a non-significant association with overall rating when complaints are held constant. The inclusion of pay raises with learning increases the complaints coefficient above solely the inclusion of learning.

title: Lab 3: Linear Regression Model Comparisons
text:
Compare the models
Model performance will be evaluated using nested-model F-tests and overall model performance

Nested-Model Comparisons


Code
nested.tests <- anova(model_1, model_2, model_3, model_4)

nested.tests

Code
nested.tests <- nested.tests |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |>
  rename(
    Residual.Df = Res.Df,
    Nested.Df = Df,
    Nested.F.stat = F,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>F)`
  )




Overall Model Performance


Code
glance1 <- glance(model_1)
glance2 <- glance(model_2)
glance3 <- glance(model_3)
glance4 <- glance(model_4)

performance <- rbind(glance1, glance2, glance3, glance4)




Combine Performance Tests, Calculate RMSE and Delta R Squared


Code
models <- c(
  "M1: Null",
  "M2: Complaints",
  "M3: Complaints + Learning",
  "M4: Complaints + Learning + Raises"
)

comparison.table <- cbind(
  Model = models,
  performance,
  nested.tests
)

comparison.table <- comparison.table |>
  mutate(Delta.R2 = r.squared - lag(r.squared),
         RMSE = c(
           sqrt(mean(residuals(model_1)^2)),
           sqrt(mean(residuals(model_2)^2)),
           sqrt(mean(residuals(model_3)^2)),
           sqrt(mean(residuals(model_4)^2)))
  ) |>
  select(
    Model,
    r.squared,
    adj.r.squared,
    RMSE,
    Delta.R2,
    Residual.Df,
    Nested.Df,
    Nested.F.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  )




Display the combined model-comparison table


Code
comparison.table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    r.squared = "R²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    Delta.R2 = "ΔR²",
    Residual.Df = "Residual Df",
    Nested.Df = "Nested df",
    Nested.F.stat = "Nested F",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared,
      Delta.R2,
      adj.r.squared,
      RMSE,
      Nested.F.stat
    ),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    decimals = 3
    ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Nested.Df, Nested.F.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(
    label="Overall Performance",
    columns = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE)
  )|>
  tab_spanner(
    label="Incremental Improvements",
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Residual.Df, Nested.Df, Nested.F.stat, Nested.p.value)
  )

Interpreting the combined table
Models 3 and 4 explain a greater proportion of variance in overall rating than model 2, but equal to each other. This suggests that the addition of opportunity for learning explains more variance than complaints alone, though that pay raises does not contribute additional information to complaints and learning. This is confirmed by the adjusted R2, which is at its highest in Model 3 but then lowers to the level of Model 2 in Model 4 when pay raise is added. That said, only adding complaints in Model 2 compared to the Null Model 1 produces a statistically significant improvement in fit. Root mean squared error decreases substantially between models 1 and 2. While Root mean squared error does decrease between models 2 and 3, and again between Models 3 and 4, the latter decrease does not appear meaningful.


Select the Best Model


Code
selected.row <- comparison.table |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = adj.r.squared,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

selected.name <- selected.row$Model

selected.model <- switch(
  selected.name,
  "M1: Null" = model_1,
  "M2: Complaints" = model_2,
  "M3: Complaints + Learning" = model_3,
  "M4: Complaints + Learning + Raises" = model_4
)


The model selected by the greatest Adjusted R2 is M3: Complaints + Learning.
Its performance is R² = 0.71, Adjusted R² = 0.69, and RMSE = 6.47 ratings.

Check Model Assumptions


Code
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(selected.model)





Regression diagnostic plots for Model 3




Code
par(op)

check_collinearity(selected.model)


# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

       Term  VIF   VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
 complaints 1.55 [1.10, 2.25]     1.25      0.64     [0.44, 0.91]
   learning 1.55 [1.10, 2.25]     1.25      0.64     [0.44, 0.91]



Evaluation of Assumptions
In the Residuals vs Fitted plot, the red line approximately runs along 0, suggesting the assumption of linearity is upheld. This plot also shows there is slight evidence of funneling suggestive of heteroscedasticity, however it does not look to be too extreme. With the Scale-Location plot, the line has multiple instances of slope, suggesting that residuals may be changing slightly as a function of fitted values. I would say that heteroscedasticity is questionable, but not horribly violated. The Q-Q residuals shows that residuals are approximately normal as though there is some deviation at the tails and ever so slightly in the middle, the residuals approximately follow the dotted line. In the Residuals vs leverage, there do seem to be some extreme values with high leverage, though since none fall in cook’s distance, they are less concerning. The variables complaints and learning had a variable inflation factor of 0.55, which is well below the typical cutoff of 5 and therefore unconcerning.
In all, while heteroscedasticity is questionable, there were no blatantly violated assumptions that would be cause for concern in interpreting Model 3.

title: Lab 3: Linear Regression Model Comparisons
text:
Report the selected model
Model 3 is the chosen most appropriate model as it has the highest adjusted R2 of all the models while limiting the root mean square error. While it is not the lowest root mean square error, Model 4 is only 1 hundredth lower, which is not a meaningful difference. This is the 2nd most complex model, though the most complex (Model 4) does not offer an increase in variation explained nor does it reduce the root mean squared error in a meaningful way. Moreover, Model 3 does not substantially violate any assumptions, allowing it to remain interpretable.

title: Lab 3: Linear Regression Model Comparisons
text:
8. Interpret the results
The selected model, M3: Complaints + Learning, explains approximately 70.8% of the variation in overall departmental ratings. Holding opportunities for learning constant, a one-point increase in a departments’ handling of complaints is associated with a significant 0.64-point increase in predicted overall workplace rating, 95% CI [0.4, 0.89]. Holding handling of complaints constant, a one-point increase in a departments’ opportunities for learning is associated with a non-significant 0.21-point increase in predicted overall workplace rating, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.49].

Overall model performance
Model 3’s adjusted R² is 0.69, and its in-sample RMSE is 6.47 overall rating points.


Substantive conclusions
This analysis illustrates how departmental workplace ratings can be investigated using several nested linear regression models. We were able to determine that handling of complaints remained a significant predictor of overall workplace rating even when opportunities for learning and pay raise were held constant. We were also able to determine that opportunities for learning and pay raise were non-significant while handling of complaints were held constant, suggesting that this is the most important factor in determining workplace ratings in this sample. Finally, opportunities for learning, but not pay raise, were able to explain additional variation above what could be explained by handling of complaints alone.
However, these finding should be considered with the following limitation in mind. The observations included in this sample are averaged among departments and not individual employees, possible obscuring important variability within those departments.
